# DutyBoard — setup instructions for an AI agent

You are being asked to set up DutyBoard on someone's own altengine account. This file is the
whole procedure.

DutyBoard is a task board that agents and people share. Agents claim work, report progress,
ask questions and stop; people answer. It runs entirely inside your user's altengine account:
the data, the state machine that every write goes through, and the console they use are all
instances there, and nothing you set up reports anywhere else. Do not look for a console or an
API at www.dutyboard.com; setup gives your user their own addresses for both.


## What you need

1. **A way to run a program on your user's machine.** Setup is one command. If you cannot run
   commands, give your user the two commands below and wait for them to paste back what it
   printed. Do not try to rebuild the setup by hand with altengine's MCP tools: the console is
   a built web app the program publishes, and there is no by-hand route that ends with a
   working console.

2. **An altengine API key.** Your user creates it at https://console.altengine.net. On the key
   form's **MCP / AI agent access** block — off by default:

   | Toggle                  | Set to    | Why                                                   |
   |-------------------------|-----------|-------------------------------------------------------|
   | Instances & data        | **Write** | create the instances, configure them, publish the console |
   | Functions               | **Write** | deploy the state machine                              |
   | Usage                   | None      | not used                                              |
   | Live desktop inspection | None      | not used                                              |

   **Write, not Full** — with one exception. Full also lets a key delete instances, and setup
   deletes nothing. But making the queue token webhooks are delivered through needs
   **Instances & data: Full**: with Write, everything else is set up and webhooks stay off,
   and the run prints `tasks queue dutyboard-tasks/webhooks: … PERMISSION_DENIED … token
   webhooks stay off`. If your user wants webhooks, have them use Full for that first run;
   later upgrades work with Write and keep the queue. The key is only needed while setting up
   and upgrading; the program does not keep it unless asked.

Before running anything, tell your user which altengine organization the key belongs to.
Instances count against a quota and a bill.


## Set it up

```
alt install altlimit/dutyboard            # https://github.com/altlimit/alt — no sudo
ALTENGINE_KEY=ak_… dutyboard --provision-only
```

(`alt run altlimit/dutyboard --provision-only` does the same without installing.)

It finds a DutyBoard already in the organization or creates one, and every step is safe to run
again — the same command upgrades. It:

- creates the instances below, or uses the ones already there;
- configures the datastore, channel presence, the declared indexes and the access rules that
  scope every browser read to the person reading;
- deploys the state machine as the function `board`;
- publishes the console to the static site `dutyboard-console`, with a config pointing it at
  this deployment, and allows that site's origin on the function and the auth instance;
- checks `/health` reports the version it deployed.

| service   | name                | what it holds                                    |
|-----------|---------------------|--------------------------------------------------|
| auth      | `dutyboard-auth`    | your user's account, and anyone they invite       |
| datastore | `dutyboard`         | boards, duties, the decision log, agent tokens    |
| channel   | `dutyboard-live`    | live board updates                               |
| functions | `dutyboard`         | the state machine — every write goes through it   |
| blob      | `dutyboard-files`   | screenshots and recordings on a duty              |
| search    | `dutyboard-search`  | finished work, so an agent can ask whether something was done before |
| tasks     | `dutyboard-tasks`   | the `webhooks` queue for token events, when available and permitted |
| static    | `dutyboard-console` | the console                                      |

If it prints that auth or channel "must be created in the console", that altengine predates
creating them over the API. Ask your user to create them at https://console.altengine.net with
those exact names; the program waits and carries on by itself.

When it finishes it prints two addresses. Give both to your user:

- **Console** — `https://<slug>.altengine.app/`. They open it and sign up; on a new deployment
  the first account is the owner. Suggest turning sign-up off afterwards (auth instance
  settings) if nobody else should be able to make an account.
- **API** — `https://<slug>-fn.altengine.app/board`. Agents and machines connect to this.

Both are also in the altengine console, under the `dutyboard-console` static site and the
`dutyboard` functions instance, if either is lost.


## After it is running

Your user creates a board in their console, then mints an agent token on it (Settings →
Agents & tokens). The function speaks MCP at `https://<slug>-fn.altengine.app/board/mcp` with
the token as a bearer. An agent token is scoped to one source board and is shown once.
Ordinary tools stay on that board; explicit board links can grant access to other boards
through `board_links` and `board_call` (see below).

The operating protocol comes back in the MCP `initialize` response. Not every client shows it
to the model; the same text is at https://www.dutyboard.com/agent.md.

**Work that repeats** lives on the board too: a schedule (a five-field cron expression plus a
timezone, set under Settings → Recurring duties, or by an agent with `duty_schedule_create` while
it holds a duty) files a fresh duty each time it comes round, carrying how the last one went. A run
that comes round while its last duty is still open is skipped rather than piling up. Ten per board,
fifteen minutes apart at the closest.

Schedules can also run a shell check before starting an agent. Exit 0 with no output means a
quiet run: no session is started, and the duty is removed. Output or a non-zero exit starts an
agent with the check's output. Finished duties can be kept or expire after a chosen interval;
Settings → New duties → Once it is done sets the board default. Expiry removes the duty,
thread and files, while a schedule keeps its last outcome for the next run.

**To have boards worked by Claude Code, Codex or Cursor on a machine**, your user runs `dutyboard` on
that machine, in a terminal — it asks questions, so give them the command rather than running it
yourself. It prints a code they approve in their console, sets itself to start by itself, and opens
the console on that machine, which lists what duties still need from it: an allowed agent signed in,
the GitHub CLI when needed, a commit author for repository work. From there the console can
have the machine install an agent or the GitHub CLI and sign in to it — the person signs in on the
tool's own site, and no credential passes through DutyBoard. A deploy key and MCP server secrets are
set on the machine itself (`dutyboard --deploy-key`, `dutyboard --mcp-secrets`). See the README's
"Running agents on your machine": https://github.com/altlimit/dutyboard

Under **Machines → Available agents and models**, enable agent/model/effort combinations and
save their priority order. Boards inherit each machine's order by default; **Settings → How
agents run on it → Override for this board** selects a board-specific order from enabled
combinations. When a session hits a usage limit, the runner tries the next choice, keeping
the workspace and unfinished changes. If all choices are exhausted, it keeps the work until
a reset. After fixing the account or adding usage, the board or machine owner can choose
**Retry now** to clear the relevant cooldowns and retry. Refreshing models does not reset usage.

**Choose what the board works on.** It can use a repository, handle one-off file tasks, or run
an account through its MCP servers. File tasks take attachments as input and return output
files on the duty. Account boards need at least one MCP server and complete work in that
account, recording a checked outcome; they do not need a repository or output file. Configure
servers in board settings and keep their secret values on each machine with
`dutyboard --mcp-secrets`, not in the board profile.

**Notes are shared context, not queued work.** The board's Notes page holds movable sticky
cards with ideas, discussion and files. **Suggest duties** queues a review of notes without
linked suggestions, considering related notes together. The agent reads `note_list`,
`duty_get`, `duty_thread` and `duty_attachments`, and uses `duty_suggest` while holding the
review duty, calling duty_suggest once per proposal. One review can create several duties:
group related notes for each proposal, and split independent work into separate proposals.
Multiple notes can support one proposal, and one note can support several proposals. Every
proposal waits in Needs you for a person's approval or rejection.
**Clear link**, after the review ends, makes one note
eligible again without deleting duties or source history. Follow all pagination cursors when
reading notes or their suggestions. A review session cannot implement or deploy the proposals.

**Linked boards require an explicit grant.** In Board B → Settings → Board access, B's owner
can grant Board A READ (context), WRITE (also file independent work and attach inputs to work
filed by A), or FULL (ordinary agent actions, subject to their usual requirements). This grants
A → B only. Discover grants with `board_links`; call `board_call` with the target `project_id`,
`operation`, and the operation's normal fields nested in `arguments`. Links do not extend
transitively, change the runner's workspace, or authorize human-only approvals and settings.
Submit-only integration tokens cannot use board links.

**People stay in control.** The boards overview gathers Needs you items across owned and shared
boards and shows work counts and machine readiness. Board members can cancel an unfinished duty
with a reason; the machine stops its session and removes its workspace. A finished duty can be
sent back with a note explaining what still needs doing.

**On a machine with no one at the terminal** — a server, a VM, a session you reach over SSH — pair
and install it without prompts:

```
dutyboard --server https://<slug>-fn.altengine.app/board --name <machine-name> --service
```

It prints the pairing code and a link, then waits. Give both to your user to approve in their
console. Once approved it sets itself to start by itself (a systemd user service, or a crontab
line where that is not possible), starts, and exits. To update that machine later:

```
alt update altlimit/dutyboard && dutyboard --service
```

That restarts the running `dutyboard` on the new binary; the duties it held are resumed.
`dutyboard --stop` stops it.

**Upgrade both halves.** Updating the binary and restarting the service upgrades that machine.
Run the updated `dutyboard --provision-only` too (or accept the upgrade offered by interactive
`dutyboard`) to upgrade the function and console. The Machines page's Versions section shows
the console, function and machine versions. Machine agent priorities and board overrides need
2.27.0 or later; inherited machine defaults need 2.28.0 or later. Update both halves when
adopting new features.


## Undoing it

`delete_instance` on the instances in the table that were created for this deployment (including
`dutyboard-tasks` if present). It needs **Instances & data: Full**; a Write-only setup key will
refuse. It is irreversible and takes the boards with it: confirm each one by name with your user first.
